Anomalies: JobSat value of 60 falls outside the 0–10 scale was initially excluded. Retired has only n = 1, and the other five job titles (red) with fewer than 30 responses are also highlighted. These job titles have wide 95% CIs and can make the means unreliable.

Diagnostic Interpretation: Small groups and invalid satisfaction responses can distort averages. The most trivial differences are at the bottom part of the chart: senior executives and founders are the most satisfied (≈8.0–8.1), while support engineers, QA/test developers and system administrators are the least (≈6.0–6.6).

Additionally, small groups may have less reliable averages, as indicated by wider confidence intervals.

Question 2¶

2(a) Descriptive Summary and Outliers

The raw salary data contain extremely high values that may distort the mean and affect the statistical tests. To reduce their influence, we applied a common upper cutoff of (Q3 + 3×IQR) to both hybrid and remote workers. Since salary should be strictly positive and its distribution is highly right-skewed, we choose to only set this upper bound for elimination of those extremely high values. We chose this conservative threshold instead of the standard (1.5 \times IQR) rule to remove only the most extreme salaries while preserving most of the data. Using the same cutoff for both groups also ensures consistent treatment and makes the salary comparison more reliable.

In [26]:
# Select Hybrid and Remote workers with valid positive salaries
raw = df[df['RemoteWork'].isin(['Hybrid', 'Remote']) &
         df[SALARY].notna() & (df[SALARY] > 0)].copy()

# Calculate the common upper cutoff using 3 × IQR
q1, q3 = raw[SALARY].quantile([0.25, 0.75])
upper = q3 + 3 * (q3 - q1)

# Remove salaries outliers above the upper cutoff
clean = raw[raw[SALARY] <= upper].copy()

# Report the cutoff and number of observations removed
print(f'Common salary upper cutoff: ${upper:,.2f}')
print('Raw group sizes:', raw.RemoteWork.value_counts().to_dict())
print('Removed by group:',
      (raw.RemoteWork.value_counts() - clean.RemoteWork.value_counts()).to_dict())

# Calculate descriptive statistics by group
def summary(frame, group):
    return frame.groupby(group)[SALARY].agg(
        ['count', 'mean', 'median', 'std', 'var', 'min', 'max',
         lambda x: x.quantile(0.25),
         lambda x: x.quantile(0.75)]
    ).rename(columns={'<lambda_0>': 'Q1',
                      '<lambda_1>': 'Q3'}).round(2)

# Display descriptive statistics before and after outlier removal
print('Raw statistics:')
display(summary(raw, 'RemoteWork'))

print('After common cutoff (used for Q2 inference):')
display(summary(clean, 'RemoteWork'))

# Extract cleaned salaries for Hybrid and Remote workers
h = clean.loc[clean.RemoteWork == 'Hybrid', SALARY].to_numpy()
r = clean.loc[clean.RemoteWork == 'Remote', SALARY].to_numpy()

# Plot raw salary distributions before removing outliers
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.boxplot([raw.loc[raw['RemoteWork'] == 'Hybrid', SALARY],
            raw.loc[raw['RemoteWork'] == 'Remote', SALARY]],
           tick_labels=['Hybrid', 'Remote'])

ax.set_yscale('log')
ax.set(ylabel='Annual salary (USD)- log scale',
       title='Salary Distributions Before Outlier Removal')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Plot salary distributions after removing outliers
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.boxplot([h, r], tick_labels=['Hybrid', 'Remote'], showfliers=False)

ax.set(ylabel='Annual salary (USD)',
       title='Salary Distributions After Outlier Removal')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

2(b) Two-sample t-test Comparison

For a two-sided two-sample t-test:

H_0: u_h = u_r

H_1: u_h =/ u_r

Here, u_h and u_r represent the population mean salaries of Hybrid and Remote workers.

Manual Calculation: x̄ = Σxᵢ/n and s² = Σ(xᵢ − x̄)²/(n − 1). Pooled SD: s_p = √{[(n₁−1)s₁² + (n₂−1)s₂²]/(n₁+n₂−2)}; t = (x̄₁ − x̄₂) / [s_p √(1/n₁ + 1/n₂)].

Since the two population groups may have unequal variance, we introduce another t-test called the Welch method for unequal variances. It can also be calculated using built-in function in the program.

In [46]:
# State the hypothesis
print('H0: Mean Hybrid salary = Mean Remote salary')
print('H1: Mean Hybrid salary != Mean Remote salary')
print('-----------------------------------------------------------------------')

# Step 1: Calculate sample sizes, means, and sample variances
nh, nr = len(h), len(r)
mh, mr = np.mean(h), np.mean(r)
vh, vr = np.var(h, ddof=1), np.var(r, ddof=1)

# Step 2: Calculate pooled variance and pooled standard deviation
sp2 = ((nh-1)*vh + (nr-1)*vr) / (nh+nr-2)
sp = np.sqrt(sp2)

# Step 3: Calculate pooled standard error and t-statistic
se_pooled = sp * np.sqrt(1/nh + 1/nr)
t_manual = (mh-mr) / se_pooled

# Step 4: Calculate degrees of freedom and two-sided p-value
df_pooled = nh + nr - 2
p_manual = 2 * stats.t.sf(abs(t_manual), df_pooled)

# Display manual calculation results
summary_2b = pd.DataFrame({
    'Group': ['Hybrid', 'Remote'],
    'Sample Size': [nh, nr],
    'Mean': [mh, mr],
    'Variance': [vh, vr],
    'Standard Deviation': [np.sqrt(vh), np.sqrt(vr)]
})

print('Descriptive Statistics')
display(summary_2b.round(2))
print('-----------------------------------------------------------------------')

manual_2b = pd.DataFrame({
    'Statistic': [
        'Pooled Variance',
        'Pooled Standard Deviation',
        'Pooled Standard Error',
        'Degrees of Freedom',
        'Manual t-statistic',
        'Two-sided p-value'
    ],
    'Value': [
        f'{sp2:,.2f}',
        f'{sp:,.2f}',
        f'{se_pooled:,.2f}',
        f'{df_pooled}',
        f'{t_manual:.5f}',
        f'{p_manual:.6e}'
    ]
})

print('Manual Pooled Calculations')
display(manual_2b)
print('-----------------------------------------------------------------------')

# Perform t-tests using SciPy built-in functions
pooled = stats.ttest_ind(h, r, equal_var=True)    # Equal variances assumed
welch = stats.ttest_ind(h, r, equal_var=False)    # Unequal variances allowed

# Compare built-in t-test results
tests_2b = pd.DataFrame({
    'Method': ['Manual Pooled', 'SciPy Pooled', 'SciPy Welch'],
    't-statistic': [t_manual, pooled.statistic, welch.statistic],
    'Degrees of Freedom': [df_pooled, pooled.df, welch.df],
    'p-value': [p_manual, pooled.pvalue, welch.pvalue]
})

print('Two-Sample t-Test Comparison')
display(tests_2b)
print('-----------------------------------------------------------------------')

print('Manual/library pooled agreement:',
      np.isclose(t_manual, pooled.statistic))
print('Difference in t-statistics:',
      abs(t_manual - pooled.statistic))
print('Difference in p-values:',
      abs(p_manual - pooled.pvalue))
print('-----------------------------------------------------------------------')

# Examine whether the equal-variance assumption is reasonable
variance_ratio = max(vh, vr) / min(vh, vr)
print('Variance ratio (larger/smaller):', round(variance_ratio, 3))

# Check if the equal-variance assumption is rejected
if variance_ratio > 2:
    print('Variances differ substantially.')
    result = welch
else:
    print('Variances are reasonably similar; pooled test may be appropriate.')
    result = pooled

print('-----------------------------------------------------------------------')

# Statistical conclusion at 5% significance
if result.pvalue < 0.05:
    print('Reject H0: There is a statistically significant difference in mean salaries.')
else:
    print('Fail to reject H0: Insufficient evidence of a difference in mean salaries.')

print('Interpretation: The p-value measures how extreme the observed t-statistic is under H0.')

2(c) Bootstrap

Resample within each group with replacement, preserving each group's sample size. The bootstrap difference distribution estimates uncertainty in $\bar X_H-\bar X_R$. Standardized values are $(\Delta_b-\Delta_{obs})/SE_{boot}$. Additionally, we need centering because ordinary bootstrap samples are generated under the observed effect, not the null.

In [31]:
# Set the number of bootstrap replications
B = 10000

# Create arrays to store bootstrap means and median differences
boot_h = np.empty(B)
boot_r = np.empty(B)
boot_med = np.empty(B)

# Resample each group with replacement, preserving group sizes
for i in range(B):
    hs = rng.choice(h, size=nh, replace=True)
    rs = rng.choice(r, size=nr, replace=True)

    boot_h[i] = hs.mean()
    boot_r[i] = rs.mean()

    boot_med[i] = np.median(hs) - np.median(rs)

boot_diff = boot_h - boot_r  # bootstrap difference
obs_diff = mh - mr  # observed difference
boot_se = boot_diff.std(ddof=1)  # standard error

# Standardize the bootstrap differences
boot_z = (boot_diff - obs_diff) / boot_se

# Figure.1: Bootstrap distributions of mean salaries for both groups
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.hist(boot_h, bins=55, alpha=0.55, label='Hybrid')
ax.hist(boot_r, bins=55, alpha=0.55, label='Remote')
ax.axvline(boot_h.mean(), color='navy', linestyle='--',
           linewidth=2, label=f'Hybrid mean: ${boot_h.mean():,.0f}')

ax.axvline(boot_r.mean(), color='darkred', linestyle='--',
           linewidth=2, label=f'Remote mean: ${boot_r.mean():,.0f}')

ax.set(xlabel='Bootstrapped mean salary (USD)',
       ylabel='Frequency',
       title='Q2(c)-1. Bootstrap Group Mean Distributions')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

# Figure 2: Bootstrap distribution of differences in mean salaries
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.hist(boot_diff, bins=60)

# Add a reference line at zero for no difference
ax.axvline(0, linestyle='--', color='black')
ax.axvline(boot_diff.mean(), color='darkred', linestyle='--',
           linewidth=2, label=f'Mean difference: ${boot_diff.mean():,.0f}')

ax.set(xlabel='Hybrid minus Remote (USD)',
       ylabel='Frequency',
       title='Q2(c)-2. Bootstrap Difference in Means')
plt.show()

# Figure 3: Standardized bootstrap distribution of mean differences
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.hist(boot_z, bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.7,
        label='Bootstrap standardized')
ax.axvline(boot_z.mean(), color='darkred', linestyle='--',
           linewidth=2, label=f'Mean: {boot_z.mean():.3f}')

# Add a standard normal distribution for comparison
zgrid = np.linspace(-4, 4, 300)
ax.plot(zgrid, stats.norm.pdf(zgrid),
        label='Standard normal reference')

ax.set(xlabel='Centered difference / Bootstrap SE',
       ylabel='Density',
       title='Q2(c)-3. Standardized Bootstrap Differences')
ax.legend()
plt.show()

# Display observed mean difference and bootstrap standard error
print(f'Observed difference: ${obs_diff:,.2f}; Bootstrap SE: ${boot_se:,.2f}')

2(d) two-sample t-test with bootstrapped data

For a valid two-sided null test, shift each group's observations to the same pooled mean before resampling. This simulates $H_0$ while preserving within-group dispersion. The bootstrap null statistic is compared to the observed Welch-style studentized statistic. A naive count of the original bootstrap differences crossing zero is not a null-hypothesis p-value.

In [30]:
# Calculate the pooled mean under H0 (equal population means)
pooled_mean = np.r_[h, r].mean()

# Shift both groups to the same mean while preserving their variability
h0 = h - h.mean() + pooled_mean
r0 = r - r.mean() + pooled_mean

# Calculate the observed Welch-style t-statistic
obs_t = obs_diff / np.sqrt(vh/nh + vr/nr)

null_t = np.empty(B)

# Generate bootstrap samples under H0
for i in range(B):

    # Resample each shifted group with replacement
    hs = rng.choice(h0, nh, replace=True)
    rs = rng.choice(r0, nr, replace=True)

    # Calculate the bootstrap t-statistic
    null_t[i] = (hs.mean() - rs.mean()) / np.sqrt(
        hs.var(ddof=1)/nh + rs.var(ddof=1)/nr
    )

# Calculate the two-sided bootstrap p-value
p_boot = (np.count_nonzero(np.abs(null_t) >= abs(obs_t)) + 1) / (B + 1)

print(f'Observed studentized statistic: {obs_t:.4f}')
print(f'Bootstrap null two-sided p-value: {p_boot:.6f}')

# 5% significance level
print(f'Bootstrap decision (alpha=.05): {"Reject H0" if p_boot < .05 else "Do not reject H0"}')

# Compare bootstrap and Welch's t-test conclusions
print(f'Bootstrap p-value: {p_boot:.6f}')
print(f'Welch p-value: {welch.pvalue:.6f}')

if (p_boot < 0.05) == (welch.pvalue < 0.05):
    print('Both tests reach the same conclusion at alpha = 0.05.')
else:
    print('The two tests reach different conclusions at alpha = 0.05.')

2(e) 95% Confidence Intervals with Formula-based and Bootstrapping Approach

The previous check for variance suggests that the two population could have similar variance and that the pooled-variance interval can be appropriate. However, since there is evidence that we may also have unequal variance for the two population groups (variance ratio of 1.443, similar variance but not necessarily), we will use the Welch's formula in this section as well just for comparison purpose. As the sample size is large, this is a more reliable method to use. Welch's unequal-variance formula uses $SE=\sqrt{s_H^2/n_H+s_R^2/n_R}$. The percentile bootstrap interval is the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the 10,000 mean differences.

In [54]:
# Observed difference in sample means
obs_diff = mh - mr

# 1. Pooled-variance CI (equal variance assumption)
# Pooled sample variance
sp2 = ((nh - 1)*vh + (nr - 1)*vr) / (nh + nr - 2)
# Pooled standard error
se_p = np.sqrt(sp2 * (1/nh + 1/nr))
# Degrees of freedom and t critical value
df_p = nh + nr - 2
tcrit_p = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df_p)
# 95% confidence interval
ci_p = (obs_diff - tcrit_p*se_p,
        obs_diff + tcrit_p*se_p)

# 2. Welch's standard error
se_w = np.sqrt(vh/nh + vr/nr)
# Welch-Satterthwaite degrees of freedom
df_w = (vh/nh + vr/nr)**2 / ((vh/nh)**2/(nh-1) + (vr/nr)**2/(nr-1))
# Find the critical t-value for a 95% confidence interval
tcrit_w = stats.t.ppf(0.975, df_w)
# 95% confidence interval
ci_w = (obs_diff - tcrit_w*se_w,
        obs_diff + tcrit_w*se_w)

# 3. Calculate the bootstrap percentile confidence interval
ci_boot = tuple(np.quantile(boot_diff, [0.025, 0.975]))

# Display results
results_2e = pd.DataFrame({
    'Method': ['Pooled t CI', 'Welch t CI', 'Bootstrap percentile CI'],
    'Lower 95% CI': [ci_p[0], ci_w[0], ci_boot[0]],
    'Upper 95% CI': [ci_p[1], ci_w[1], ci_boot[1]]
})

results_2e['Contains zero?'] = (
    (results_2e['Lower 95% CI'] <= 0) &
    (results_2e['Upper 95% CI'] >= 0)
)

print(f'Observed mean difference (Hybrid - Remote): ${obs_diff:,.2f}')
display(results_2e.round(2))

2(f) Examine the Median Salaries

Mood's test checks whether group medians differ, using counts above and below a common median. The bootstrap median difference distribution gives a separate, approximate two-sided test by centering its sampling distribution at the observed median difference; the two tests need not agree because they use different statistics and approximations.

In [36]:
# Perform Mood's median test on cleaned Hybrid and Remote salaries
mood = stats.median_test(h, r)

# Calculate the observed difference in median salaries
med_obs = np.median(h) - np.median(r)

# Calculate a two-sided bootstrap p-value
# Center the bootstrap median differences around the observed difference
p_med = (np.count_nonzero(
    np.abs(boot_med - med_obs) >= abs(med_obs)
) + 1) / (B + 1)

# Calculate the bootstrap 95% CI for the median difference
med_ci = np.quantile(boot_med, [0.025, 0.975])


# Display Mood's median test and bootstrap results in a DataFrame
results_2f = pd.DataFrame({
    'Statistic': [
        'Hybrid median',
        'Remote median',
        'Mood test statistic',
        'Mood test p-value',
        'Bootstrap two-sided p-value',
        'Bootstrap 95% CI (lower)',
        'Bootstrap 95% CI (upper)'
    ],
    'Value': [
        np.median(h),
        np.median(r),
        mood.statistic,
        mood.pvalue,
        p_med,
        med_ci[0],
        med_ci[1]
    ]
})

display(results_2f)


# Compare the two p-values at alpha = 0.05
print('Mood test rejects H0:', mood.pvalue < 0.05)
print('Bootstrap test rejects H0:', p_med < 0.05)

if (mood.pvalue < 0.05) == (p_med < 0.05):
    print('Both tests reach the same conclusion.')
else:
    print('The two tests reach different conclusions.')

print('----------------------------------------------------------------------')
print('Note: Discrete medians and ties may cause the p-values to differ.')

# ==========================================================
# Question 3(b): One-way ANOVA hypothesis testing
# ==========================================================

# H0: All three population mean salaries are equal
# H1: At least one population mean salary is different

# Perform one-way ANOVA using the cleaned salary groups. Assume equal variances.
anova = stats.f_oneway(*groups)

# Check the equal-variance assumption using the variance ratio
variances = [np.var(g, ddof=1) for g in groups]
variance_ratio_3 = max(variances) / min(variances)

print(f'Variance ratio (largest/smallest): {variance_ratio_3:.3f}')

# Assess whether the group variances are reasonably similar
if variance_ratio_3 > 2:
    print('Variances differ substantially.')
else:
    print('Variances are relatively similar.')

# Display ANOVA and assumption-check results
print('One-way ANOVA F:', anova.statistic)
print('ANOVA p-value:', anova.pvalue)

# 5% significance level
print('Decision alpha=.05:',
      'Reject equal means' if anova.pvalue < 0.05
      else 'Do not reject equal means')

print('ANOVA tests whether at least one group mean differs.')

# ==========================================================
# Question 3(c): Bootstrap salary comparison by education
# ==========================================================

B = 10000
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# Bootstrap the mean salary for each education group
boot_means = np.empty((B, 3))

for i in range(B):
    for j, g in enumerate(groups):
        boot_means[i, j] = rng.choice(g, len(g), replace=True).mean()

# Calculate pairwise differences in bootstrap means
pairs = [(0, 1), (0, 2), (1, 2)]
pair_labels = ['Bachelor - Master',
               'Bachelor - Professional',
               'Master - Professional']

pair_diffs = np.column_stack([
    boot_means[:, i] - boot_means[:, j] for i, j in pairs
])

obs_means = np.array([g.mean() for g in groups])
obs_pair = np.array([obs_means[i] - obs_means[j] for i, j in pairs])

pair_ses = pair_diffs.std(axis=0, ddof=1)
pair_z = (pair_diffs - obs_pair) / pair_ses

colors = ['steelblue', 'orange', 'seagreen']

# Figure 1: Bootstrap mean distributions for three groups
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))

for j, lev in enumerate(levels):
    ax.hist(boot_means[:, j], bins=55, alpha=0.4,
            color=colors[j], label=lev)

    ax.axvline(boot_means[:, j].mean(), color=colors[j],
               linestyle='--', linewidth=2)

ax.set(xlabel='Bootstrapped mean salary (USD)',
       ylabel='Frequency',
       title='Q3(c)-1. Three Education-Group Mean Distributions')

ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))

for j, label in enumerate(pair_labels):

# ==========================================================
# Question 3(d): Bootstrap ANOVA hypothesis test
# ==========================================================

grand=np.concatenate(groups).mean()
null_groups=[g-g.mean()+grand for g in groups]
null_f=np.empty(B)
for i in range(B):
    samples=[rng.choice(g,len(g),replace=True) for g in null_groups]
    null_f[i]=stats.f_oneway(*samples).statistic
p_fboot=(np.count_nonzero(null_f>=anova.statistic)+1)/(B+1)

results_3d = pd.DataFrame({
    'Method': ['Original ANOVA', 'Bootstrap ANOVA'],
    'F-statistic': [anova.statistic, anova.statistic],
    'p-value': [anova.pvalue, p_fboot],
    'Reject H0 (0.05)?': [anova.pvalue < 0.05, p_fboot < 0.05]
})

print('ANOVA Comparison')
display(results_3d)

print('Original ANOVA p:',anova.pvalue)
print('Bootstrap-null ANOVA p:',p_fboot)
print('Bootstrap decision alpha=.05:', 'Reject H0' if p_fboot<.05 else 'Do not reject H0')
print('Comparison: discrepancies can reflect skew, unequal variances, finite bootstrap error, or ANOVA assumption violations.')
